interactions.summary: Jiang completes the paradox answer by saying God always forgives, but precisely for that reason must intervene when corruption prevents ordinary people from living faith, hope, and love; a student links this to illness, Covid, and the limits of money and power.
A long YouTube comment is read aloud presenting Dante as a persecuted heroic prophet and anti-corruption fighter, after which Jiang says the rhetoric is exaggerated but the essential picture is true.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Quoted online comment read in class, then interpreted by Jiang

speaker_notes.note: These segments are quoted material from a commenter, not Jiang's own prose, though Jiang endorses the broad interpretation afterward.

claims.claim: Jiang says Dante's real difference from church orthodoxy is that there is no final risk: God always forgives, but that forgiveness increases responsibility to live faith, hope, and love.
If society becomes so corrupt that an ordinary person cannot live faith, hope, and love, Jiang says divine intervention becomes necessary as an act of love.
A student suggests plague or illness strips away confidence in money and power and redirects dependence toward God, which Jiang accepts as a useful opening to the discussion.
Jiang uses the read-aloud comment to characterize Dante as a prophet whose life is marked by alienation, persecution, and exile.
Jiang says Peter's and Beatrice's tirades in Paradiso are not anomalies but promises of divine judgment once society becomes unjust enough.

signature_moments.moment: God's limitless forgiveness becomes the reason intervention is mandatory, not optional.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It flips mercy from passive tolerance into active responsibility and closes Jiang's theological paradox.

signature_moments.moment: The prophet is defined by alienation, persecution, and exile.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns Dante's biography into a model for why his anger and judgment claims should be taken seriously.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's term for God's corrective action when society becomes too corrupt for ordinary people to live well.
A condition of exile, persecution, and conflict produced by fidelity to faith, hope, and love in an unjust society.

chronology_notes.note: This packet closes the lecture's opening theological setup and explicitly pivots into reading Dante as a prophet of Florentine injustice for the rest of the class.

uncertainty_notes.note: The read comment is rhetorically heated and historically compressed; Jiang explicitly marks it as exaggerated while keeping its core framing of Dante as a persecuted prophet.
